Your height above the ground where you stand. Visibility is calculated from this height. 1.7 m is eye level on the ground; on a high floor, a roof or a lookout enter the real height, otherwise nearby buildings and terrain wrongly hide the targets.

PointAndIdentify identifies the target the camera is pointed at (settlement, mountain, tower and more) and checks against a terrain model whether it is really visible from where you stand.

Crosshair
Aim the center of the crosshair at the target. The screen shows only a target that is inside the crosshair circle, both in direction and in height angle (aiming at the sky or at the street selects nothing), and in direct line of sight; the crosshair is then green. With no such target it is red. The crosshair grows with the zoom, and the circle in which targets are recognized grows with it.

Pointing down
When the camera axis meets the ground close to you (the street below you, or a phone lying on a table), the app shows only the current city: the settlement nearest in the direction the camera was turned to (within 30° of it; if there is none, the nearest settlement overall). A visible target in the crosshair that is not farther than the aimed ground takes precedence. Looking down quickly from a hill at a distant settlement does not start the mode. The nearer the aim is to the ground below you, the nearer the target: lowering the camera never selects a farther target. The title shows the diameter of the current-location circle: twice the distance at which the camera axis meets the ground, calculated over the terrain from your real height above the aimed ground. On the edge of a 100 m hill, lowering the camera shrinks the circle down to about 500 m. The mode also applies whenever the aimed ground is within 1.5 km of you, at any angle.

Stability
The shown target is replaced by another only when the other is clearly better for about half a second, and a target that has just left the crosshair stays on the screen for a moment, so small hand shakes do not swap places.

Hidden targets
Tap inside the crosshair to list every target inside the circle: visible ones first, then ones hidden by terrain or without terrain data, ranked by offset from the center.

Find
The Find button (next to the gear) searches for a place by free text: a private point such as “Home”, a settlement name, an address, or coordinates such as 32.07, 34.78. When the place is on the screen, a small red dot appears exactly on it: steer the dot into the center of the crosshair. When it is off the screen, a cyan arrow at the outer edge of the crosshair shows where to turn the camera; when the place is inside the circle, a ring also appears. A line under the title shows its range and azimuth. To stop, open Find and choose Stop finding.

Zoom
The bar at the side of the screen: minimum at the bottom, maximum at the top, with the current zoom next to the handle. You can also pinch the screen. Beyond the camera's own zoom, an extra calculated (digital) zoom applies, at lower quality. In Settings you can place the bar on the right or on the left.

Compass
On the opposite side of the bar: the red arrow points to true north and the yellow mark at the top is the camera direction. Below it is the camera heading in degrees from true north.

Data
At the bottom: observer position and accuracy, height with the vertical angle, and the target details: type, height, position, range, azimuth, angle and line-of-sight clearance. All lines are always shown; a dash means the value is not known. The target position appears only while the phone is raised for aiming; held flat, only your current position is shown.

Capture
Saves a photo to the gallery (DCIM/PointAndIdentify) with the crosshair and data burned in, cut to the shape of the screen view, and position and direction in the photo metadata (EXIF).

Settings (gear icon)
Switch the language between Hebrew and English, the zoom bar side, private points, your height above the ground, and the app update check.

Height above ground
Visibility is calculated from your height above the terrain: 1.7 m by default (eye level on the ground). On a high floor, a roof or a lookout, enter the real height in Settings; otherwise nearby buildings and terrain wrongly hide the targets. The terrain model also includes buildings, so a small blocker (under 5 m) is ignored as model noise. The app can also measure your height with the barometer and GPS (Settings); it uses this only to raise the height, and only by a safe margin.

Private points
Save a place of your own, for example “Home”, from your current location or from coordinates. A saved point is identified like any other target when you aim at it from another place, including the line-of-sight check. Tap a saved point to edit its name or delete it.

At launch
The app checks the compass (magnetic field, calibration, stability; hold the phone still for a few seconds) and looks for a newer version. The version check also repeats when you return to the app after more than 10 minutes, and retries after a minute if it failed (for example without a network). A message appears only when something needs attention.

Anonymous counting
To count installations and versions, the app downloads one tiny public file from the release page: once on the first run of a new installation, and once per installed version. The request carries no identifier, location or personal data (like any download, the server sees the network address). Totals are shown on the statistics page of the site.

Exit
The ✕ button in the bottom row closes the app completely.

Terms on the screen

Observer position: your GPS coordinates (latitude, longitude).

Position accuracy: the estimated GPS error in meters. The smaller the number, the more accurate the position.

Height: your height above sea level: ground height from the elevation model plus 1.7 m (eye level).

Vertical angle: the camera angle above the horizon (plus) or below it (minus).

Type: the kind of target, for example settlement, peak or tower. Height: the height of the target above sea level.

Target position: the coordinates of the target.

Range: the straight-line distance from you to the target, in kilometers.

Azimuth: a direction in degrees, clockwise from true north: 0° north, 90° east, 180° south, 270° west. The number under the compass is the camera direction.

Azimuth to target: the true direction from you to the target. When the camera is aimed correctly it is close to the camera direction.

Angle to target: the angle at which the target lies above the horizon (plus) or below it (minus), as seen from where you stand. If it is close to the camera's vertical angle, the camera height is aimed correctly.

Clearance: the smallest difference between the line of sight to the target and the ground, along the whole way, in meters. Positive: clear line of sight, and the larger it is the safer the view. Negative: terrain blocks the view. Dash: cannot be calculated.

Hidden by terrain: a ridge or hill blocks the line of sight to the target. Such targets appear only in the list that opens when you tap the crosshair.

No terrain data: the elevation data for the area has not been downloaded yet, so visibility cannot be determined.

Terrain tiles: how many terrain pieces (of those needed around you) are already on the device. Targets: the number of targets in the database.

Compass: OK (field in µT): the magnetic field strength measured by the sensor. The normal range is about 25 to 65 µT; outside it there is interference from metal or a magnet.

Offset from cross: in the identify window, how many degrees the target is from the center of the crosshair.

Accuracy and limits
“Visible” is an estimate from a terrain model, not a confirmation that you saw the target. The elevation model (SRTM) is accurate to a few metres up to a few tens of metres and does not fully include trees and buildings. The check ignores a blocker up to 5 m below the line of sight, and the terrain within 60 to 150 m of a target is not tested, so the target does not block itself. These are estimated values that were not validated in the field.
The camera heading depends on the device compass, which can be disturbed by nearby metal or a magnet even after the start-up check.
The counters on the statistics page count downloads of files from GitHub, not installs or users. The SHA-256 check of an update verifies file integrity only; the authenticity of the app is verified by Android's signature check at install.
If downloading data from the main source fails, the app tries a second source (jsDelivr) for the same files. A file is accepted only when its SHA-256 matches the manifest.
